wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e111.summary: This paragraph joins two pieces. It opens with a stray one-sentence reply that belongs to the end of the preceding question: an a priori demonstration is not of substance itself. It then poses the third principal question of the Prologue: whether theology, as theologians have it under the common law (de communi lege), is scientia proprie dicta. Two arguments for yes follow. (1) Every truth-bearing intellectual habit about necessary truth is understanding, wisdom or science (Ethics VI). Theology is not understanding (it is not self-evident) or wisdom (which includes understanding and science), so it is science. (2) The theologian has a more perfect habit than the layperson, who has faith, and with respect to necessary truth nothing is more perfect than faith except understanding, wisdom or science.
claims: Every truth-bearing intellectual habit about necessary truth is understanding, wisdom or science (argument).
The theologian's habit is more perfect than the layperson's faith (argument).

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e146.summary: Third argument: 1 Corinthians 12 speaks of the gift of 'the word of knowledge (scientia)'. Being a supernatural gift, it can only concern necessary theological truths, so there is a science of them.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e157.summary: Argument to the contrary: a habit that rests precisely on authority is not scientia proprie dicta, and theology rests on authority.
claims: A habit resting only on authority is not strict science.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e162.summary: Surveys the opinions, beginning with affirmative ones. The first (Aquinas's subalternation model) holds that once the first principles of theology are held by faith, without evident knowledge, we acquire strict science of the conclusions that follow. Some sciences proceed from principles known by natural light (geometry), others from principles known by the light of a higher science (optics from geometry). Theology proceeds from principles known by the higher science of God and the blessed: as music believes principles handed down by arithmetic, sacred doctrine believes principles revealed by God.
claims: Theological conclusions are known scientifically from believed principles (reported).
Theology is subalternated to the knowledge of God and the blessed (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e211.summary: Others argue that denying theology is a science would detract from its dignity and contradict the truth. Theology excels all sciences in certainty, resting on a supernatural light that cannot deceive or be deceived, and in the dignity of its matter, which exceeds reason. Other sciences are its handmaids, and it judges them. Its expositors call it a science (Wisdom 10, 1 Corinthians 12, Augustine De Trinitate XIII), and the intellectual habits are only five (Ethics VI).
claims: Theology excels other sciences in certainty and dignity (reported).
Scripture and Augustine call theology a science (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e249.summary: A second affirmative opinion: theology is true science of principles as well as conclusions, acquired by the power of faith and the light of the agent intellect. Theology is not understanding, prudence or art, and not faith either, since, per Augustine (De Trinitate XIV), many abound in faith but not in this science.
claims: Theology is science of both principles and conclusions (reported).
Theology and faith are distinct habits (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e276.summary: Supporting argument: habits with distinct acts are distinct. The act of faith is to assent without evidence at the will's command, while the act of theology is to defend and strengthen faith (Augustine).
claims: The act of faith is assent without evidence at the will's command (reported).
The act of theology is to defend and strengthen faith (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e293.summary: The opinion's proofs that theology is science. (1) What can be known not to entail anything impossible can be known, and any theological truth can be known not to: an objection errs in form (and can be solved) or in matter (and can be denied). (2) An intellect that can know a subject under the ratio containing all knowable truths can know them evidently, and God under the ratio of deity contains all theological truths and can be known abstractively by us. This is because discursive reasoning ends in knowledge of God, and the intellect distinguishes God from creatures. (3) The first in every genus is maximally such, and theology is first among sciences.
claims: What can be known not to entail the impossible can be evidently known (reported).
God can be known abstractively by us under the ratio of deity (reported).
Theology is the first of sciences (reported).
concepts: God under the ratio of deity

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e343.summary: Fourth proof: otherwise the theologian would have no more perfect habit than an old woman (vetula), which seems unfitting.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e350.summary: A third affirmative opinion: both principles and conclusions are known in theology, though not by the light of faith or of nature, but by a higher light intermediate between faith and the light of glory. Otherwise one believer would not have clearer, only firmer, knowledge of matters of faith than another, contrary to Augustine's remark that many lack this science, which consists in clarity of knowledge.
claims: Theology involves a light intermediate between faith and glory (reported).
Some believers have clearer knowledge of matters of faith than others (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e374.summary: Answers the reply that faith admits of increase: then faith and this science would always be equal, so whoever excelled in faith would excel in the science, which contradicts Augustine.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e383.summary: Ockham argues against the conclusion shared by all three opinions. By God's absolute power there could be strict science of theological truths, and perhaps some have it de facto for some truths, but not according to the common course. Everything evidently known is either self-evident, made known through self-evident propositions, or known by experience through intuitive cognition, mediately or immediately. Articles of faith are none of these. Not self-evident, or unbelievers would know them. Not derived from self-evident propositions, or any unbeliever properly questioned would assent (Augustine, Retractationes). Not from experience, since every intuitive cognition a believer has, an unbeliever can have too.
claims: By absolute power there could be strict science of theological truths, but not under the common law.
Everything evidently known is self-evident, derived from self-evident propositions, or known by experience through intuitive cognition.
Articles of faith are not self-evident, derivable from self-evident propositions, or known by experience.
Believers and unbelievers have the same intuitive cognitions.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e431.summary: Further arguments. If necessary articles of faith were strictly known, contingent articles would be evidently known as well, so anyone could know that they are in charity or that Christ's body is on the altar, which is false. Then, against the claim that faith is presupposed by this science: two judicative habits about the same object are never ordered so that one necessarily presupposes the other, and here faith and science would concern the same object. Infused faith is also not necessarily presupposed. A habit contributes to another only through its act, and acquired faith inclines to the same act as infused faith, so the scientific habit could be acquired through acquired faith alone.
claims: No one can evidently know that they are in charity or that Christ's body is on the altar.
Two judicative habits about the same object are never ordered so that one presupposes the other.
A habit contributes to another only through its act.
Infused and acquired faith incline to the same act.
Infused faith is not necessarily presupposed by any theological science.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e509.summary: Arguments against the first opinion in particular. The habit of principles is better known and more evident than the habit of conclusions, because that through which something is known is known better. So it is impossible that the principles are merely believed while the conclusions are known.
claims: Principles are more evidently known than the conclusions derived from them.
Conclusions cannot be scientifically known if their principles are merely believed.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e527.summary: Further: opinion of principles relates to opinion of conclusions as evident knowledge of principles relates to evident knowledge of conclusions. One cannot hold a conclusion as opinion because of premises without holding the premises as opinion, so one cannot evidently know conclusions through principles without evidently knowing the principles.
claims: Evident knowledge of conclusions through principles requires evident knowledge of the principles.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e545.summary: Further: whoever evidently knows a conclusion through principles evidently knows that it follows from necessary propositions, and so evidently knows those principles.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e555.summary: Against the second opinion: the distinction of acts does not prove that theology is a distinct habit or strict science. Every act a believer has, an unbeliever trained in theology could have: defending and strengthening the faith, persuading, answering heretics. Yet such a person plainly lacks strict science.
claims: An unbeliever trained in theology can perform all the theologian's acts except believing.
The acts of defending and strengthening faith do not prove strict science.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e581.summary: Further: it would follow that someone could know these truths evidently from purely natural means. No habit inclines to another habit's act except through its own act, so whatever can be known through infused faith can be known without it if its act can be elicited without it. The act of faith can be had from natural means through acquired faith.
claims: Whatever can be known through a habit can be known without it if its act can be had otherwise.
The act of faith can be elicited from purely natural means through acquired faith.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e601.summary: Against the third opinion: every infused habit has an act that can be elicited by some acquired habit (as shown inductively for charity, faith and hope). But no naturally acquired habit inclines to an act of knowing articles of faith, because any natural habit a believer can have, an unbeliever can have too.
claims: Every infused habit has an act that some acquired habit can also produce.
Every naturally acquired habit of a believer can be had by an unbeliever.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e627.summary: Further: every act of the intellect is evidently known to it, intuitively. So this act of knowing would be evident, and no theologian could doubt having it, but many great theologians deny having such an act.
claims: Every act of the intellect is intuitively and evidently known to it.
Many theologians deny having scientific knowledge of articles of faith.
concepts: intuitive cognition of one's own acts

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e643.summary: Confirmation: a believer is certain of believing, and there is no more reason for a believer than for a knower to be certain, so whoever knows an article would be certain of knowing it.
claims: No one can believe something without being certain that they believe it.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e656.summary: Answers an objection based on the first question, that an act can be intuitively known while its contingent truths are not evidently known. One may be unable to tell one's act apart from another and still know one has it if it is intense. Someone with intense love and delight may doubt whether love and delight are really distinct but is certain of loving and delighting. So any theologian who believed and knew articles would be certain of both and could evidently know that they know them.
claims: One can know that one has an intense act without being able to discriminate it from others.
A theologian who scientifically knew articles of faith would know that they know them.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e701.summary: Further: whoever evidently knows a proposition cannot dissent from it by command of the will alone. They would need a stronger counter-reason or to forget something evident. But a theologian, however learned, can dissent from articles of faith by will alone, without a stronger reason (none from falsehoods could outweigh evident truths) and without forgetting. So the theologian has no evident knowledge of them.
claims: Evident knowledge cannot be dissented from by will alone.
A theologian can dissent from articles of faith by the will's command alone.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e727.summary: Turns to negative opinions. One (the philosophers') holds that we can naturally attain all science possible to us, so nothing is merely believable that cannot be evidently known. This cannot be refuted by natural reason, only by authority.
claims: The philosophers' view that all knowledge is naturally attainable cannot be refuted by natural reason, only by authority.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e749.summary: Another negative opinion, which Ockham holds true: although articles of faith can be evidently known, they are not known by us in this state under the common law. So theology as we ordinarily learn it is not strict science of them, though there could be science of some.
claims: Articles of faith are not evidently known by us in this state under the common law.
Theology as commonly learned is not strict science of the articles of faith.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e765.summary: Sets out the plan: first, show that every habit besides faith that a believing theologian acquires about articles of faith can be acquired by an unbeliever; second, determine what habit besides faith the theologian acquires.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e776.summary: Proof of the first point by parsimony: no habit should be posited in us unless shown by some act manifest to us or by Scripture's authority, and no such habit can be shown either way.
claims: No habit should be posited unless evidenced by a manifest act or by Scripture.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e789.summary: Proves the minor premise. Every act except believing that a believer has, an unbeliever raised among Christians or trained in theology can have, as shown inductively. And Scripture attributes nothing but faith to us regarding articles of faith.
claims: Every act of a believer except believing can be had by a trained unbeliever.
Scripture attributes only faith to us regarding articles.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e803.summary: Concludes: every actual cognition, complex or incomplex, that a believer can have, apart from faith alone, an unbeliever can have.
claims: Apart from faith, a believer has no actual cognition an unbeliever cannot have.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e812.summary: On the second point, reports an opinion that theological study produces a habit beyond faith that is not adhesive (causes no assent) but only 'declarative'. It is the intellectual virtue of wisdom (Ethics VI), the light and understanding the saints mention. Its arguments: the agent intellect with propositions as instruments causes an intellectual habit other than faith, which was already present; and the theologian has acts beyond believing, such as giving reasons, defending against the impious, strengthening the pious, speaking wisdom among the perfect.
claims: Theological study produces a non-adhesive, declarative habit beyond faith (reported).
This declarative habit is wisdom (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e847.summary: Further argument of the opinion: something is acquired from such study, or it would be pointless, whether an act or a habit, and either way a habit results.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e854.summary: The opinion argues the habit is not adhesive: otherwise it would be opinion, since it cannot be science or wisdom about articles of faith, and it would make the believer fearful about theological truths.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e865.summary: The opinion argues it is declarative: a habit that makes the intellect better 'imagine' something without any adhesion is declarative, providing explanation of terms, resolution of tangled arguments, examples and guidance, and support from probable reasons and inductions.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e878.summary: The opinion argues it has the character of wisdom: metaphysics is wisdom yet in some of its acts is only declarative.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e888.summary: Ockham rejects the opinion: some habit is acquired, but it is not wisdom. Any habit a believer acquires by such study an unbeliever could acquire by similar study, and an unbeliever plainly lacks true wisdom about theological matters.
claims: The declarative habit from theological study is not wisdom.
An unbeliever lacks true wisdom about theological matters.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e910.summary: Further, according to Aristotle in Ethics VI wisdom is not without understanding and science (the citation continues in the next paragraph).
claims: Wisdom is not without understanding and science.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e917.summary: Completes the argument: 'wisdom is science and understanding of the most honorable things', but the declarative habit can exist without understanding and science, since it can coexist with faith alone and exist in an unbeliever, who can perform all the acts of reasoning, defending and strengthening that a believer can. Confirmation: wisdom cannot coexist with error about the same thing, but this habit coexists with error about articles of faith.
claims: The declarative habit can exist without understanding and science.
Wisdom cannot coexist with error about the same thing.
The declarative habit coexists with error about articles of faith.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e946.summary: Ockham's own answer on the theologian's habits. Regarding articles of faith, the theologian increases acquired faith if it preceded study, or acquires it if a believer; an unbeliever lacks this. Beyond that, in fact and for the most part, any student of theology, believer, heretic or unbeliever, acquires many scientific habits acquirable in other sciences. He also acquires many scientific habits of consequences proper to theology, and apprehensive habits of all terms and propositions, whether knowable or only believable. Through these, without faith, one can perform every act possible to a theologian under the common law except believing: preaching, teaching, strengthening.
claims: Theological study increases or produces acquired faith in believers.
Any student of theology acquires scientific habits from other sciences, habits of theological consequences, and apprehensive habits.
These habits suffice for every theological act except believing.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e992.summary: These habits, besides faith and the naturally acquirable habits of consequences, are not strict science. Nothing is evidently known whose assent requires faith, since a habit inclining to evident knowledge depends on faith no more than the reverse. By common agreement, no one can assent to articles of faith without faith.
claims: Nothing whose assent requires faith is evidently known.
No one can assent to articles of faith without faith.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1010.summary: Answers the objection that then there would be no supernatural knowledge besides faith. 'Supernatural knowledge' has two senses. As knowledge that cannot be naturally acquired, no such knowledge besides infused faith is necessary for us under the common law. As knowledge of truths that can be evidently known only supernaturally, not from natural means, such knowledge is necessary for us besides faith.
claims: Under the common law, the only necessary non-naturally-acquirable knowledge is infused faith.
Knowledge of truths evidently knowable only supernaturally is necessary besides faith.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1033.summary: Answers the first argument of the 'declarative habit' opinion: through the agent intellect and propositions, acquired faith is sometimes increased and sometimes acquired. It is not infused, and one need not always already have faith in the matter.
claims: The agent intellect with propositions increases or produces acquired faith.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1053.summary: Concedes that the other two arguments prove that some habit other than faith is acquired.
claims: Some habit other than faith is acquired through theological study.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1058.summary: Answers the argument that the habit is not adhesive: an acquired adhesive habit would not be opinion, if opinion is distinguished from faith. So no adhesive habit about articles of faith is acquired other than infused and acquired faith.
claims: No adhesive habit about articles of faith is acquired other than faith.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1071.summary: Concedes that the habit may be called declarative.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1076.summary: Answers the last argument: the habit other than faith does not have the character of wisdom, since it can coexist with error and exist naturally without understanding and science. On metaphysics, he distinguishes, as in the first question, between knowledge of many ordered items and knowledge inclining immediately to one complex. In the first sense not every part of metaphysics is wisdom: answering sophistical arguments is not formally wisdom, though evident refutation presupposes science. If a theologian could evidently defend and strengthen the faith, he would necessarily have wisdom, but that is not naturally possible. In the second sense metaphysics can be called wisdom, as the next question will explain.
claims: The non-faith habit of theology is not wisdom.
Not every part of metaphysics is wisdom.
Evident defense of the faith would require wisdom, which is not naturally possible.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1111.summary: Answers the first opinion's argument from subalternation. Even in a subalternate science no one evidently knows the conclusions except through experience or evidently known premises. It is empty to say 'I know conclusions because you know the principles I believe on your word', and likewise 'puerile' to say I know theology's conclusions because God knows the principles I believe because he reveals them.
claims: In subalternate sciences, conclusions are evidently known only through experience or evident premises.
Knowing conclusions because God knows the principles is 'puerile'.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1138.summary: Answers the dignity argument: it does not detract from our theology's dignity that its conclusions are not evidently known, just as it does not for its principles. The argument from excellence in certainty and dignity of matter would equally prove that the principles are evidently known.
claims: Lack of evident knowledge does not detract from theology's dignity.
The excellence argument would prove too much.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1162.summary: Distinguishes certainty as adhesion from certainty as evidence: theology excels in the first sense, not in the second.
claims: Theology excels in certainty of adhesion, not in certainty of evidence.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1171.summary: Answers the confirmation: other arts are called theology's handmaids, and it judges them, because of the greater truth of what it knows and the firmer adhesion.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1180.summary: Answers the appeal to the saints: they call theology a science by extending the name to certain knowledge and to apprehensive habits of things that of themselves could be objects of science and wisdom.
claims: The saints use 'scientia' in an extended sense for theology.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1196.summary: Answers the argument that the truth-bearing intellectual habits are only five: Aristotle lists five kinds among naturally acquired habits. For him faith as a whole is not truth-bearing, since it can concern falsehoods. Besides those, there is a truth-bearing habit under which nothing false can fall: faith regarding theological articles, whether infused or acquired.
claims: Aristotle's five intellectual habits are naturally acquired.
Faith regarding theological articles, infused or acquired, is truth-bearing.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1218.summary: Alternative reply: Aristotle speaks only of evident and certain habits, and theology regarding articles of faith is certain but not evident.
claims: Theology regarding articles of faith is certain but not evident.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1228.summary: Answers the second opinion's first argument: as to every judicative habit, theology is science or faith. For every act besides believing, apprehensive habits with knowledge of consequences suffice, as experience shows. If this is called a logical habit, Ockham replies that logic covers the nature of consequences in general, not particular consequences. Every science uses logic as an instrument to know its own consequences in particular: the astronomer, not the logician, knows that 'the earth is between sun and moon, so the moon is eclipsed' is valid.
claims: For all theological acts except believing, apprehensive habits plus knowledge of consequences suffice.
Logic concerns consequences in general, not in particular.
Each science knows its own particular consequences, using logic as an instrument.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1259.summary: Answers the argument from non-contradiction: something is evidently known if it is evidently known that nothing impossible follows from it.
claims: What is evidently known not to entail anything impossible is evidently known.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1266.summary: But this is not known of any article of faith: it is not evident that an article is not the antecedent of a consequence inferring something impossible. Every bad argument does err in form or matter, but this cannot be evidently known. 'The divine essence is the Father; the divine essence is the Son; so the Son is the Father' errs in form, yet no one under the common law can evidently know that, just as no one can know that one absolute thing is several really distinct relative persons. 'God is immortal; no man is God; so no man is immortal' errs in matter with a false minor, which theologians only believe to be false.
claims: It is not evident that no article of faith entails something impossible.
That trinitarian paralogisms err in form cannot be evidently known under the common law.
That 'no man is God' is false is only believed, not known.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1303.summary: Answers the second proof by denying the major premise, to be treated in another question.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1308.summary: Also denies the minor: in this life God cannot be known by us under the proper ratio of deity by a simple cognition in which God alone is known.
claims: In this life God cannot be known under the proper ratio of deity by a simple cognition.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1317.summary: Answers the first supporting proof: discursive reasoning ends in a complex proposition, previously unknown, whose terms were all already known by incomplex knowledge. Reasoning is only between complexes, so it never yields incomplex knowledge of any term, nor apprehension of the complex, which can be had beforehand, but only judicative knowledge. Someone reasoning from creatures to God presupposes incomplex knowledge of God and creature and acquires only assent to 'God is an infinite being' or 'something is the highest being'.
claims: Discursive reasoning yields only judicative knowledge of a complex.
Reasoning never produces incomplex knowledge of terms.
Reasoning from creatures to God yields assent to propositions like 'God is an infinite being'.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1366.summary: Answers the second proof: the intellect distinguishes God from creatures by having one proper composite concept and denying every creature of it. Having concluded that some being is first and highest, it has the concept 'infinite and highest being', proper to God, and knows that no creature falls under it.
claims: We distinguish God from creatures through a proper composite concept, not a simple concept of God.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1384.summary: Asks why God is then understood more than before, since we have only a composite concept that is not God. Ockham answers that God is understood because we have a proper concept naturally apt to supposit for God alone, the only way God can be naturally known in this life. God does not immediately terminate our act of understanding in this state; only the concept does. This agrees with Gregory on Ezekiel: however far the mind advances in contemplating God, it reaches not what God is but something beneath him.
claims: God is understood through a proper concept that supposits for God alone.
In this life God does not immediately terminate our act of understanding; the concept does.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1410.summary: This holds on the fictum theory, where a concept has objective being produced by the act of understanding. On the alternative theory, where the concept predicated for things is the act of understanding itself and universals are acts inhering in the mind, the intellect reaches a composite of many acts of understanding. Each separately grasps other things as much as God, but the whole composite grasps only God, so God alone is its object. Such a composite cognition is not unfitting, but it does not suffice for possessing theological truths.
claims: On the fictum theory, a concept has objective being produced by the act.
On the intellectio theory, concepts and universals are acts inhering in the mind.
A composite of common acts of understanding can have God alone as its object.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1449.summary: Raises Gregory's authority against the second theory: on that view the mind could advance in contemplation to deity itself, not merely to what is beneath God. Ockham replies that Gregory's point, on that view, is that under the common law the mind's every cognition in this life is such that it, or some part of it, grasps other things as much as God, so it never reaches precisely what God is but also what is beneath him.
claims: Every cognition of God in this life, or some part of it, also grasps things other than God.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1480.summary: Answers the third proof: as to the relevant part, theology is neither first, last nor middle among strict sciences, since it is not a strict science in that respect.
claims: Theology in its faith-dependent part is not ranked among strict sciences.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1491.summary: Answers the fourth (vetula) proof: the theologian knows many things the old woman does not, but regarding a single article she may sometimes have as perfect a cognition as the theologian, while lacking much else.
claims: About a single article of faith, a lay believer may know as perfectly as a theologian.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1503.summary: Answers the argument for the third opinion: Ockham concedes that no one has clearer, meaning more evident, knowledge of articles than another, since no one has evident knowledge of them. This does not oppose Augustine, who extends the name 'science'. Many excel in faith without excelling in this science of expounding and defending Scripture, so superiority in knowing an article does not lie in clarity.
claims: No one has more evident knowledge of articles of faith than another.
Augustine extends the name 'scientia'.
Superiority in theological knowledge does not consist in clarity of cognition.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1525.summary: Answers the objection that faith and science would then be equal: they would not be, because this 'science' includes many habits beyond faith.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1534.summary: Answers the first principal argument: every evident truth-bearing habit about necessary truth is wisdom, science or understanding, but an inevident truth-bearing habit can be faith, which theology largely is. There is also a habit about such truths that is not properly truth-bearing, being apprehensive rather than judicative, which part of theology is.
claims: Theology is largely an inevident truth-bearing habit, namely faith.
Part of theology is a merely apprehensive habit.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1554.summary: Answers the second principal argument: the theologian's total habit is more perfect than a layperson's, but not always regarding particular articles.
claims: The theologian's total habit is more perfect, but not necessarily about each article.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1561.summary: Answers the third principal argument: the Apostle extends 'wisdom' and 'science' to the habits by which one knows how Scripture should be expounded, defended and strengthened.
claims: Paul uses 'wisdom' and 'knowledge' in an extended sense.

wo8uy7-d1e142-d1e1570.summary: Asks what probable reasons adduced for articles of faith accomplish: faith, opinion, science or nothing. They increase acquired faith, though not infused faith, and sometimes generate it. That is why some are said to hold opinions as firmly as others know: such 'opinion' is really faith, not opinion as distinguished from faith.
claims: Probable reasons for articles of faith increase or generate acquired faith, not infused faith.
Firm 'opinion' in matters of faith is really acquired faith.

wo8uy7-d1e142.summary: Prologue question 7, the third principal question, asks whether theology as theologians have it under the common law is scientia proprie dicta. Ockham reviews three affirmative opinions: Aquinas's subalternation model (conclusions known from principles believed on God's authority), an opinion making theology a habit distinct from faith that knows principles and conclusions, and an opinion positing a light intermediate between faith and glory. He rejects them all. Evident knowledge comes only from self-evident propositions, from what is derived from them, or from intuitive experience, and articles of faith are none of these, since unbelievers have the same intuitions. Conclusions cannot be known from merely believed principles; an unbeliever can perform all theological acts except believing; one would be introspectively certain of such knowledge; and one could not dissent from it by will alone. He accepts the negative view that, though articles could be known by God's power, they are not known by us under the common law. The theologian's habits besides faith are acquired faith, scientific habits from other disciplines, habits of theology's particular consequences, and apprehensive habits. Unbelievers can have all of these except faith, and none is wisdom. Replies clarify that theology excels in certainty of adhesion rather than evidence, that logic covers only general consequences, that trinitarian paralogisms cannot be evidently refuted, and that in this life God is known only through a proper composite concept, explained on both the fictum and intellectio theories of concepts.
claims: Theology under the common law is not scientia proprie dicta of articles of faith.
Evident knowledge requires self-evidence, derivation from self-evident propositions, or intuitive experience.
Conclusions cannot be scientifically known from merely believed principles.
Apart from faith, a believing theologian has no habit an unbeliever cannot have.
Theology excels in certainty of adhesion, not of evidence.
In this life God is known only through proper composite concepts.
